scenes.tts: Every winter, crews drag dredges along the bottom of the Chesapeake Bay. They sample blue crabs at about one thousand five hundred sites. From one winter to the next, the estimated number of crabs can change by more than one hundred million. So how many crabs can it really hold?
scenes.caption: Every winter, crews drag dredges along the bottom of the Chesapeake Bay. They sample blue crabs at about 1,500 sites. From one winter to the next, the estimated number of crabs can change by more than 100 million. So how many crabs can it really hold?
scenes.visual: Bay outline with survey site marks and a dredge arrow; two winter bars with a gap labelled more than 100 million (estimate, not to scale); a big question mark.
scenes.narration: Every winter, crews drag dredges along the bottom of the Chesapeake Bay. They sample blue crabs at about 1,500 sites. From one winter to the next, the estimated number of crabs can change by more than 100 million. So how many crabs can it really hold?

scenes.tts: A population is all the members of one species living in the same area at the same time. The blue crabs in the Bay this winter are a population. Biotic factors are living parts of the environment, like predators and disease. Abiotic factors are nonliving parts, like temperature and salinity, the salt level. A limiting factor keeps a population from growing larger.
scenes.visual: A box of crab tokens labelled population; living factors (green) and nonliving factors (orange) push in on the box as arrows.
scenes.narration: A population is all the members of one species living in the same area at the same time. The blue crabs in the Bay this winter are a population. Biotic factors are living parts of the environment, like predators and disease. Abiotic factors are nonliving parts, like temperature and salinity, the salt level. A limiting factor keeps a population from growing larger.

scenes.tts: Suppose ten bacteria land in a dish of fresh food. Each one splits in two every thirty minutes. Now there are twenty, then forty, eighty, one hundred sixty, and three hundred twenty. This is exponential growth. On a graph, it makes a J shape. No real population can keep this up for long.
scenes.caption: Suppose 10 bacteria land in a dish of fresh food. Each one splits in two every 30 minutes. Now there are 20, then 40, 80, 160, and 320. This is exponential growth. On a graph, it makes a J shape. No real population can keep this up for long.
scenes.visual: Bars 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320 rise one per step; a J curve joins the tops.
scenes.narration: Suppose 10 bacteria land in a dish of fresh food. Each one splits in two every 30 minutes. Now there are 20, then 40, 80, 160, and 320. This is exponential growth. On a graph, it makes a J shape. No real population can keep this up for long.

scenes.tts: Then limits set in. Food runs short, and crowding makes competition and disease worse. The curve bends into an S shape and levels off. The level it settles near is the carrying capacity. Carrying capacity is the largest population an environment can support over time. If few animals move in or out, births and deaths are about equal there. The numbers still go up and down a little. That is dynamic equilibrium.
scenes.visual: Axes (model, made-up units): the J rises, red limits label, the curve bends to an S, a gold dashed line marks carrying capacity, small wobbles along it.
scenes.narration: Then limits set in. Food runs short, and crowding makes competition and disease worse. The curve bends into an S shape and levels off. The level it settles near is the carrying capacity. Carrying capacity is the largest population an environment can support over time. If few animals move in or out, births and deaths are about equal there. The numbers still go up and down a little. That is dynamic equilibrium.

scenes.tts: Carrying capacity is not one number stamped on a species. It changes when the environment changes. More food, a mild winter, or more hiding places can raise it. A hard freeze or the loss of marsh grass can lower it. People change it too. Crabbing removes crabs from the Bay each year.
scenes.visual: The same model: the gold line steps up with green causes, steps down with red causes, and the curve follows; a chip for crabbing removing crabs.
scenes.narration: Carrying capacity is not one number stamped on a species. It changes when the environment changes. More food, a mild winter, or more hiding places can raise it. A hard freeze or the loss of marsh grass can lower it. People change it too. Crabbing removes crabs from the Bay each year.

scenes.tts: So how many crabs can the Bay hold? There is a largest number it can support over time. But that number moves as conditions change. This is probably why the crab count rises and falls. Remember this rule. Carrying capacity is not fixed. It moves with the environment.
scenes.visual: The question, then three chips in a chain, then the rule in large type.
